title: Increasing the effectiveness and efficiency of the supply chain in individual prevention.
summary: The STEEVI study investigates how different lifestyle programs impact the health and quality of life of people with early signs of chronic disease. The study focuses on programs that promote physical activity, nutrition, smoking behavior, and behavioral training and that can be prescribed by doctors via a prevention prescription. 750 participants in eight regions of Baden-Württemberg are taking part in the study. Depending on the group, they receive programs of varying intensity (from 8 to 36 hours, with or without personal coaching and group meetings). The aim is to find out which programs are particularly effective and efficient in improving quality of life and reducing health costs.
conditions: Participants with lifestyle-related risk factors (exercise, diet, obesity, smoking) and initial signs of disease (conspicuous biomarkers, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, lipometabolic disorders, chronic back pain, knee/hip osteoarthritis, osteoporosis).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Adults aged 18 years and older with AOK insurance
• Enrolled in the selective contract for family doctor-centred care (HZV)
• Lifestyle-related risk factors (physical inactivity, unbalanced eating behavior, smoking)
• Elevated biomarkers and/or (first-time) diagnosis of hypertension, lipid metabolism disorders, pre-diabetes, obesity, chronic back pain and hip and knee osteoarthritis
Exclusion criteria:
• Insufficient physical capacity (able to walk for at least 20 minutes)
• End organ damage
• Unable to train on training machines
• Insufficient knowledge of German
• BMI ≥ 35 kg/m2
